analysis.one_liner: Taxes imported oil at up to $28 a barrel so foreign crude costs more than domestic.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee, and no vote was ever taken before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would place an excise tax on crude oil and refined petroleum products imported into the United States. The tax would rise as world oil prices fall, up to $25 a barrel on crude, plus $3 a barrel on refined products, so that imported oil would never sell below a government-set "energy policy price." Oil bought for export would be exempt. The effect would be to make gasoline and other petroleum products more expensive for American consumers whenever world prices were low, while guaranteeing domestic oil producers a protected, higher price for their own crude.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic oil producers, who would be shielded from cheap foreign oil and could sell their crude at prices closer to the government-set floor. The federal Treasury would also collect the tax.

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes an excise tax on the first sale or use in the United States of imported crude oil and refined petroleum products [S2][S3].

For crude oil, the tax equals the amount by which $25 a barrel exceeds the average international price of crude over the previous four weeks, so the tax grows when world oil prices fall and disappears when they reach $25 [S3].
Refined petroleum products would carry an additional $3.00 per barrel on top of the crude-oil charge [S3].
Petroleum purchased for export would be tax-free, concentrating the cost on oil sold to American buyers [S2][S3].
The bill makes the imported-oil tax deductible for income tax purposes, softening the cost to the companies that pay it [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Anyone who buys gasoline, diesel, heating oil, or other petroleum products in the United States would pay more whenever world oil prices are below the $25 target, since importers pass the tax through at the pump and in home-heating bills. Importers and refiners that rely on foreign crude would also bear collection and compliance costs, though the tax would be deductible.

drawbacks.text: The tax would raise fuel costs for consumers and businesses precisely when world oil is cheapest, functioning as a price floor that transfers money from drivers and households to domestic oil producers [S3].
Because it is a tariff-style tax on imports, it invites retaliation and raises costs for industries that depend on imported petroleum [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall on ordinary consumers: a variable tax of up to $28 a barrel on imported oil works out to roughly 65 cents a gallon at the maximum, hitting hardest when world prices are low. The gains go to domestic oil producers, who would be guaranteed a protected market. The tax is deductible against income tax, which limits the burden on the oil companies themselves but not on the people buying fuel.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it; the bill died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Nickles introduced the bill on January 14, 1991, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Finance the same day [S1][S5].
The Finance Committee never reported the bill, and no further action appears in the record through the end of the 102nd Congress [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: American consumers of gasoline and heating oil are better off, because the import tax that would have raised their fuel costs when world oil was cheap never became law. Foreign oil suppliers and import-dependent refiners also avoided the charge.

for.name: Sen. Don Nickles
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to tax imported crude oil and refined petroleum products.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never reported it out for a floor vote.

against.name: Sen. Lloyd Bentsen
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or floor action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsor and its sole cosponsor were Republicans; the Democratic-controlled Finance Committee never acted on it.

industries.note: The bill would set an effective price floor of up to $25 a barrel for foreign crude, letting domestic producers sell their own oil at the protected higher price. Their gain comes directly out of American fuel consumers' pockets.

Refiners and importers of foreign crude would pay the new tax on every barrel and face registration, reporting, and penalty rules, though the tax is income-tax deductible and would largely be passed to customers. Those relying on cheap imports would see their cost advantage eroded.
The tax would make their crude more expensive in the U.S. market, reducing demand for it relative to domestic oil.
